blind_reasoning: Sudden severe pain, NSAID use, rigid abdomen and free gas under both hemidiaphragms is a perforated viscus until proven otherwise; she is tachycardic and febrile and needs resuscitation, antibiotics and urgent surgical transfer tonight, not observation or a morning CT.

second_defensible.why: No other option is safe; A, C and D all delay definitive surgical care for a perforation with early sepsis.

cueing.why: B is the longest option and the only one that bundles several actions (NBM, fluids, analgesia, antibiotics, two phone calls), which marks it as the 'do everything' answer.

accuracy.why: Pneumoperitoneum on erect CXR with peritonism is a surgical emergency; management described in B is standard Australian practice for a rural site without a surgeon.

level_fit.why: Recognising free gas and initiating resuscitation and retrieval is squarely within PGY2 scope when covering a rural site overnight.

notes_for_reviewer: Sound item, but trim B or lengthen the distractors so the key is not the obvious composite answer. Consider also stating that the on-call GP is contacted (currently the stem mentions the GP but B does not).

blind_reasoning: Night pain worse lying flat, prior breast cancer, T8 tenderness, brisk reflexes, difficulty standing and new urinary retention is suspected metastatic spinal cord compression; urgent whole-spine MRI (not just the symptomatic level) within 24 hours is the standard.

second_defensible.why: CT with contrast (B) is only the fallback when MRI is contraindicated or unavailable; the stem explicitly provides 24-hour imaging.

cueing.why: Options are of similar length and structure; 'urgent' and 'whole spine' are the tested discriminators rather than cues.

accuracy.why: Consistent with NICE/eviQ MSCC guidance; nothing wrong in the stem.

level_fit.why: An intern should recognise the MSCC red flags and request the imaging, though in practice they would also phone the registrar urgently and start dexamethasone.

notes_for_reviewer: Good item at the stated difficulty. Explanation should mention immediately informing the registrar/oncology and dexamethasone, so the intern is not left thinking imaging alone is the whole action.

blind_reasoning: Age 65 and over is the risk factor most Australian mild head injury pathways (NSW ITIM, NEXUS II; CCHR and NICE when LOC/amnesia present) use to lower the threshold for CT; the fall from standing, a soft frontal haematoma and a mild headache are not criteria.

second_defensible.why: Under NEXUS II 'scalp haematoma' is itself a CT criterion, so a candidate using that rule could argue B. More importantly, under the Canadian CT Head Rule and NICE this patient (no LOC, no amnesia, GCS 15) does not strictly meet any CT criterion, so the premise of the lead-in ('indicates that a CT head is required') depends on which rule is applied.

cueing.why: Options are parallel and short; no grammatical or length cue.

accuracy.why: The stem does not name a decision rule. CCHR applies only with LOC, amnesia or disorientation, and NICE requires LOC/amnesia plus age over 65 for the 8-hour CT; the NSW/ITIM mild head injury pathway and NEXUS II do treat age over 65 alone as a CT indication. The key is defensible but the lead-in's certainty is guideline-dependent.

level_fit.why: Applying a head injury CT rule is appropriate PGY2 scope in a rural ED.

clarity.why: State which guideline or pathway the candidate should apply (for example the NSW ITIM adult mild head injury guideline) so that age over 65 is unambiguously the sole positive criterion.

notes_for_reviewer: Key A is what most Australian clinicians would answer, but the item needs the decision rule named in the stem or lead-in; otherwise B (scalp haematoma, NEXUS II) is arguable and purists will say no CT is mandated by CCHR/NICE at all.

blind_reasoning: Unrecordable INR, prolonged aPTT, undetectable fibrinogen and very high D-dimer with a normal platelet count 90 minutes after a brown snake bite is classic venom-induced consumption coagulopathy, which defines systemic envenoming and mandates antivenom.

second_defensible.why: DIC from sepsis is implausible at 90 minutes with normal platelets and no sepsis; warfarin would not consume fibrinogen; a clotted sample would not produce this coherent pattern with a raised D-dimer.

cueing.why: C is the only option containing 'venom', which links directly to the stem, but given the item is a recall/interpretation item at difficulty 1 that is the intended association rather than an unfair cue.

accuracy.why: Pattern, timing and pressure immobilisation are accurate; platelets typically normal in brown snake VICC.

level_fit.why: Interpreting the coagulation screen after snakebite is appropriate for any prevocational doctor in rural SA.

cultural_safety.why: Respectful portrayal; ALO involved with his agreement, family present, no stereotype.

notes_for_reviewer: Straightforward and accurate. Explanation should spell out that VICC is the indication for antivenom and that the ALO/family involvement is good practice.

blind_reasoning: Fever with neutrophils 0.2 nine days after R-CHOP is febrile neutropenia; Therapeutic Guidelines require cultures (line and peripheral) and empirical IV piperacillin+tazobactam within 60 minutes without waiting for results or seniors.

second_defensible.why: Observation, oral antibiotics with discharge, or waiting for cultures are all unsafe in neutropenic fever.

cueing.why: B is slightly longer but the distractors are plausible-sounding actions rather than throwaways; not materially cueing.

accuracy.why: Timing, antibiotic choice and culture practice match eTG and Australian consensus.

level_fit.why: Starting empirical antibiotics for febrile neutropenia while awaiting senior input is expected PGY2 behaviour.

notes_for_reviewer: Good difficulty-1 item. Explanation could note the MASCC score is not used to delay IV therapy and that the consultant should still be informed when free.

blind_reasoning: Under the 2019 Australian paracetamol guideline the two-bag infusion is continued if at completion ALT has risen above 50 U/L or doubled from baseline, or paracetamol remains detectable; only D (ALT 28 to 120) meets that. An isolated mildly raised bilirubin with normal ALT and INR is not a criterion.

second_defensible.why: A and B show trivial ALT change within the reference range; C has a bilirubin rise alone, which does not trigger continuation.

cueing.why: Options are parallel data sets; no cue.

accuracy.why: Consistent with the MJA 2019 guideline (Chiew et al) and PIC practice.

level_fit.why: Deciding whether to stop NAC after PIC advice is a realistic after-hours junior task.

notes_for_reviewer: Accurate. Target difficulty of 5 seems overstated; this is a fairly direct recall of the stop criteria. The explanation should quote the exact criteria (ALT over 50 or doubled; paracetamol detectable) and mention re-phoning PIC.

blind_reasoning: Low TSH with low-normal T4 and low T3 in a man recovering from severe pneumonia with no thyroid symptoms is non-thyroidal illness (sick euthyroid); TFTs should not have been ordered acutely and are repeated after recovery.

second_defensible.why: Treating in either direction or ordering antibodies and a nuclear scan in an acutely unwell patient is not defensible.

cueing.why: Options are similar in length; the two drug options are symmetrical.

accuracy.why: Pattern and recommended action are correct.

level_fit.why: Writing a discharge plan for an incidental abnormal result is core intern work.

notes_for_reviewer: Good item. Explanation should mention Choosing Wisely: avoid TFTs during acute illness.

blind_reasoning: A mildly raised but flat hs-troponin (48 to 51, delta under 20 percent) in an 80-year-old with CKD and an acute COPD exacerbation, no chest pain and an unchanged ECG, is chronic or demand myocardial injury, not an acute coronary syndrome; continue treating the exacerbation and discuss with the physician.

second_defensible.why: Dual antiplatelets plus enoxaparin or urgent angiography would be harmful without a dynamic rise or ischaemic features; serial troponins until normal would never end in CKD.

cueing.why: C is longest but A is also long; distractors read as serious alternatives.

accuracy.why: Interpretation of a non-dynamic troponin in CKD and acute illness is correct.

level_fit.why: Appropriate for either PGY level.

notes_for_reviewer: Sound. Explanation should define the delta concept and note the aspirin he is presumably already on for IHD continues.

blind_reasoning: A single hs-troponin drawn 1 hour after symptom onset cannot rule out MI; a repeat sample and ECG at 2 to 3 hours is required before labelling the pain benign, and nothing in the stem justifies empirical anticoagulation or antiplatelet loading.

second_defensible.why: Though PE deserves thought (post-op, COCP), starting therapeutic enoxaparin on day 2 post-laparoscopy without imaging or a risk score is not the best next step; A dismisses the pain prematurely.

cueing.why: Options are balanced; D is only marginally longer.

accuracy.why: Consistent with hs-troponin rule-out protocols (single-sample rule-out requires at least 3 hours from onset).

level_fit.why: Appropriate intern-level decision; the intern would also inform the surgical registrar.

notes_for_reviewer: Good. Explanation should acknowledge PE risk and that a structured PE assessment is part of the reassessment; also note that reassurance to the nurse is not yet possible.

blind_reasoning: An asymptomatic, non-pregnant, non-diabetic woman with a positive dipstick after catheter removal has asymptomatic bacteriuria, which eTG and Choosing Wisely say should not be treated; antibiotics are withheld and she is reassessed if symptoms or fever appear.

second_defensible.why: Both antibiotic options treat a non-indication; recatheterising to obtain a specimen is harmful.

cueing.why: No length or wording cue; B is of similar length to the antibiotic options.

accuracy.why: Correct. Routine dipsticks themselves are discouraged, which the explanation could note.

level_fit.why: Declining an inappropriate antibiotic request is core PGY2 stewardship.

notes_for_reviewer: Good stewardship item. Explanation should mention cancelling/ignoring the culture result if asymptomatic and feeding back about routine dipsticks.

blind_reasoning: Acute fluctuating inattention with visual hallucinations in a febrile, tachycardic, hypotensive, hypoxic man with a diabetic foot infection is hyperactive delirium from sepsis and hypoxia; the daughter's history excludes alcohol withdrawal and the picture is not primary psychosis.

second_defensible.why: B relies on an assumption the stem explicitly contradicts; C lacks inattention/fluctuation features of psychosis; D ignores clear sepsis physiology.

cueing.why: A is marginally longer and includes 'such as sepsis or hypoxia', which maps to the vitals, but the item is an interpretation item and the mapping is the point.

accuracy.why: Correct; the patient also meets escalation criteria, which the explanation should emphasise.

level_fit.why: Appropriate for PGY2.

cultural_safety.why: The nurse's alcohol assumption is presented as the bias to reject and the daughter's account is respected; portrayal is otherwise respectful. Option D (Country/family distress) is a plausible-sounding but stereotyped distractor; acceptable as a teaching point but an Aboriginal reviewer should confirm the framing.

notes_for_reviewer: Good anti-bias item. Recommend Aboriginal health reviewer sign-off on option D wording, and the explanation should state the next step is sepsis escalation (RDR/MET) rather than sedation.

blind_reasoning: A verbally agitated but non-violent patient with pain, noise and probable methamphetamine withdrawal should first receive verbal de-escalation, analgesia and offered oral sedation, with the on-call doctor called in; IM droperidol with two nurses restraining, locking him in, or police removal are unsafe or unlawful first steps.

second_defensible.why: No other option meets Australian de-escalation-first guidance.

cueing.why: C is the longest and the only compound, measured option; A, B and D read as obviously punitive or dangerous.

accuracy.why: Correct and consistent with eTG psychotropic and SA Health restraint policy; it also addresses the ward's staffing limits.

level_fit.why: Appropriate PGY2 scope.

notes_for_reviewer: Correct key, but the distractors are too weak for the stated difficulty and the key is clearly the longest; consider replacing B or D with a more tempting option (e.g. oral diazepam alone without addressing pain, or IM olanzapine without de-escalation).

blind_reasoning: A rising withdrawal score to 16 with hallucinations, tachycardia and hypertension signals evolving delirium tremens, which needs immediate medical review, score-driven benzodiazepine and senior involvement; delegating to the nurse, deferring to a morning CT or using IM haloperidol alone is unsafe.

second_defensible.why: A delays review of a deteriorating patient; C and D miss the treatment.

cueing.why: B is the longest, multi-part option and the only one that includes escalation, which is a recognisable 'correct answer' pattern.

accuracy.why: Correct; symptom-triggered diazepam escalation and GP/senior notification are standard. Thiamine already given.

level_fit.why: Appropriate for both levels.

clarity.why: Clear, though the prioritisation element (whether to abandon the cannula) is minor and 'finish quickly' is a reasonable hedge.

notes_for_reviewer: Key correct; editor should balance option lengths and could make A more tempting (e.g. give an extra 20 mg diazepam and review in 30 minutes) so the item tests the need for face-to-face review rather than spotting the longest option.

blind_reasoning: Confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia in a malnourished heavy drinker is Wernicke encephalopathy, which requires high-dose parenteral thiamine (eTG: 500 mg IV three times daily) now; oral low-dose thiamine or a multivitamin is inadequate and glucose before thiamine can precipitate deterioration.

second_defensible.why: Only D is a treatment dose by a reliable route; B is actively harmful if given before thiamine and his glucose is normal.

cueing.why: Options are short and parallel; two thiamine options force the candidate to know dose and route.

accuracy.why: Dose and route match eTG and AMH for suspected Wernicke encephalopathy.

level_fit.why: Prescribing thiamine is squarely intern scope.

cultural_safety.why: Portrayal is respectful: his decision to stop, family support, ALO involvement with consent. No stereotype beyond the clinical fact of alcohol dependence, which is handled without judgement.

notes_for_reviewer: Good. Explanation should state that thiamine must precede any glucose-containing fluid and that magnesium should be checked/replaced.

blind_reasoning: He demonstrates understanding, retention, weighing and communication of the decision, so he has capacity; a capacitous refusal must be respected, and the junior's role is to explore the fear, re-explain, involve family and the ALO, and keep the cardiologist and senior informed. The Mental Health Act cannot be used to treat a physical illness and refusal does not equal incapacity.

second_defensible.why: B, C and D are respectively unlawful, misuse of the MHA, and abandonment.

cueing.why: A is by far the longest option and reads as the balanced, process-rich answer; B and C contain overtly wrong legal assertions that signal they are wrong.

accuracy.why: Legally and ethically correct for SA (Consent to Medical Treatment and Palliative Care Act 1995; MHA 2009 does not cover physical treatment).

level_fit.why: Within PGY2 scope, though the explanation should emphasise immediate senior/cardiologist notification of the refusal.

cultural_safety.why: Respectful; family and ALO involvement offered rather than imposed, and his reasoning is presented as rational.

notes_for_reviewer: Correct and important content, but at difficulty 1 with two self-evidently wrong distractors and a very long key, the item is close to a giveaway. Shorten A and make D more tempting (e.g. 'document his refusal, obtain written consent for discharge and arrange GP review').

blind_reasoning: Acute-onset disorientation, inattention and hallucinations in a woman with pyelonephritis who is now febrile, tachycardic and hypotensive is delirium from worsening sepsis; she meets Rapid Detection and Response criteria and needs bedside assessment, escalation and the physician phoned, not a psychiatric pathway.

second_defensible.why: A, B and D all treat a medical emergency as a psychiatric one.

cueing.why: C is the longest option and the only one naming physiological deterioration; the psychiatric options are internally consistent with the nurse's red herring but read as a set of three wrong answers.

accuracy.why: Correct; vitals meet SA Health RDR escalation criteria.

level_fit.why: Appropriate PGY2 scope.

cultural_safety.why: Portrayal respectful; no stereotype, mother's history valued.

notes_for_reviewer: Key is correct and important. Suggest balancing option length and swapping D for a medically-flavoured but wrong option (e.g. give IV haloperidol and continue current antibiotics) to raise discrimination.

blind_reasoning: Passive death wish, hopelessness, feeling a burden, poor intake and sleep in a 19-year-old with a prolonged admission is possible suicidal ideation and warrants a direct, structured risk enquiry tonight and escalation; it should not be reframed as adjustment, opioid effect or insomnia.

second_defensible.why: A, C and D each defer assessment and would be unsafe.

cueing.why: Options are of similar length and each proposes an action, so no length cue; B's 'this evening' is the tested discriminator.

accuracy.why: Correct.

level_fit.why: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts and escalating is core intern practice.

notes_for_reviewer: Good item. Explanation should include what a direct enquiry covers (plan, means, intent, protective factors) and ward safety measures.

blind_reasoning: A psychotic woman intending to walk to a highway at 02:00 cannot safely be allowed to leave despite voluntary status; the lawful path is to keep her safe under observation while the on-call doctor assesses for a Level 1 inpatient treatment order under the SA Mental Health Act 2009 and mental health triage is contacted.

second_defensible.why: Letting her leave ignores a duty of care and the Act's provisions; IM olanzapine as a means of detention is chemical restraint without authority; police custody is not appropriate for an inpatient.

cueing.why: D is far longer than the other options and the only one that names a lawful process; the other three are clearly inappropriate.

accuracy.why: Consistent with SA MHA 2009 (a medical practitioner may make a Level 1 ITO; care and control pending examination is permitted).

level_fit.why: Appropriate; the intern escalates rather than making the order alone.

notes_for_reviewer: Key correct. Shorten D and strengthen one distractor (e.g. 'persuade her to stay and offer her regular antipsychotic, documenting she remains voluntary') so the item discriminates at difficulty 2.

blind_reasoning: Under the SA Mental Health Act 2009 a Level 1 inpatient treatment order requires examination by a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner within 24 hours of the order (video examination permitted in rural areas) to confirm, vary or revoke it; the order was made at 15:00 so that examination is the time-critical task.

second_defensible.why: Clerking is routine, non-urgent transfer booking and GP letters are not time-critical and do not affect the lawfulness of detention.

cueing.why: A is somewhat longer and includes the specific time, but B is of comparable length; the time detail is the tested knowledge.

accuracy.why: Statutory timeframe and video provision are correctly stated for SA.

level_fit.why: Knowing the 24-hour examination requirement is expected of SA prevocational doctors working under the Act, and the task is to arrange, not to perform, the examination.

clarity.why: Clear, though 'tonight' slightly conflicts with a deadline of 15:00 tomorrow; the intent (arrange it now) is understandable.

notes_for_reviewer: Good SA-specific item. Distractors C and D are weak; consider replacing one with 'formal notification to the Public Advocate' or 'completing the Level 2 order yourself' as a more tempting legal distractor.

blind_reasoning: BMI 14.3, heart rate 42, temperature 35.4, postural hypotension and hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia and hypomagnesaemia are medical admission criteria for anorexia nervosa with high refeeding risk; she needs monitored admission, electrolyte replacement and thiamine, discussed with the physician, not outpatient management.

second_defensible.why: All outpatient options are unsafe with these physiological parameters.

cueing.why: C is slightly longer but all options are single-sentence plans; no strong cue.

accuracy.why: Admission thresholds match RANZCP/Australian eating disorder guidance. With bradycardia 42 and hypothermia at a site without ICU, transfer may be needed, which the explanation should mention.

level_fit.why: Recognising medical instability and escalating is intern scope.

notes_for_reviewer: Sound. Explanation should address her preference to go home (capacity, involving the physician and if needed the MHA/guardianship pathway) and the possibility of transfer to a monitored bed.

blind_reasoning: A 1 g amitriptyline ingestion with drowsiness, tachycardia, mydriasis and dry mucosa is a potentially lethal tricyclic overdose; cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG for QRS widening and immediate senior notification come before suturing or psychiatric assessment.

second_defensible.why: A and C delay life-threatening toxicology management; D delays for a paracetamol level and gives charcoal to a drowsy patient without airway consideration.

cueing.why: B is longer but each option is an action sequence; not materially cueing.

accuracy.why: Correct; consistent with eTG toxicology and PIC advice.

level_fit.why: Appropriate intern prioritisation.

notes_for_reviewer: Good. Explanation should mention sodium bicarbonate for QRS over 100 ms, PIC call, and that psychiatric assessment follows medical stabilisation.

blind_reasoning: A recently bereaved, isolated older man with heavy alcohol use, weight loss, insomnia and suicidal thoughts with an identified means at home is high risk; the intern must not discharge on a hypnotic and should communicate the risk to the registrar and arrange urgent mental health assessment. No-harm contracts are not evidence-based.

second_defensible.why: A follows an unsafe phone suggestion; B and C discharge a high-risk patient without assessment.

cueing.why: Options are of comparable length; D's 'before any discharge' is the content tested.

accuracy.why: Correct; aligns with graded assertiveness and SA Health suicide prevention pathways.

level_fit.why: Appropriate; tests speaking up to a senior, which is a prevocational competency.

notes_for_reviewer: Good. B and C are weak; consider making C 'means restriction plus GP review tomorrow' more tempting by adding a safety plan, so the discriminator is the need for assessment tonight.

blind_reasoning: A previous suicide attempt is the single strongest predictor of future suicide; female sex, younger age and employment are either protective or associated with lower risk.

second_defensible.why: None of the other options is a risk factor in this direction.

cueing.why: Options are parallel; no cue beyond the obviousness of the content.

accuracy.why: Correct.

level_fit.why: Basic recall appropriate for both levels.

notes_for_reviewer: Accurate but all three distractors are rated 1, so the item will not discriminate even at difficulty 1. Consider distractors that are genuine risk factors but weaker than a prior attempt (e.g. recent relationship conflict, access to means) to make the 'strongest' judgement real.

blind_reasoning: A positive pregnancy test with bleeding and pain, hCG 1,800 IU/L and a transvaginal scan showing no intrauterine or adnexal pregnancy is a pregnancy of unknown location; ectopic pregnancy is neither confirmed nor excluded and she needs serial hCG and specialist follow-up.

second_defensible.why: A and B assert outcomes the scan cannot establish and both discharge from follow-up; D overstates the findings since no adnexal mass is seen.

cueing.why: Options are of similar length; A and B each include a 'requiring' clause that mirrors C's structure.

accuracy.why: Correct. hCG 1,800 is around the TVUS discriminatory zone, which increases concern for ectopic but does not confirm it; the item handles this correctly.

level_fit.why: Interpretation and referral are appropriate PGY2 GP-term tasks.

notes_for_reviewer: Good item. Explanation should note that PUL with hCG near the discriminatory level in a symptomatic patient warrants same-day obstetric discussion, safety-netting and repeat hCG at 48 hours.

blind_reasoning: At 80 hours ulipristal acetate 30 mg is the only oral emergency contraceptive licensed and effective up to 120 hours and it remains more effective than levonorgestrel, including in women over 70 kg or BMI over 26; copper IUD would be most effective but is declined. Levonorgestrel single or doubled is for use within 72 hours and the Yuzpe regimen is obsolete.

second_defensible.why: C (double-dose LNG) is advised for higher body weight only within 72 hours; A and D are inferior at 80 hours.

cueing.why: Options are short and parallel.

accuracy.why: Consistent with FSRH/Family Planning Alliance Australia guidance. UPA efficacy may be reduced above 85 kg/BMI 30, which the explanation should mention while confirming UPA still beats LNG.

level_fit.why: Appropriate PGY2 prescribing decision.

clarity.why: Clear; the clinical details (no breastfeeding, no progestogen use, timing in cycle) are correctly supplied.

notes_for_reviewer: Sound. Explanation should add that the copper IUD was the most effective option and should be re-offered, that UPA is OTC in Australia, and to advise no progestogen for 5 days and a pregnancy test in 3 weeks.
